newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma shrugs off US sanctions, exiles applaud.
newsitem.headline: Burma shrugs off US sanctions, exiles applaud.

text.p: A top Burmese military leader on Tuesday shrugged off a U.S. decision to impose economic sanctions on Burma and analysts questioned the effectiveness of the move meant to punish Rangoon for human rights abuses.

"It's not a problem for us," Lieutenant-General Khin Nyunt, Secretary One of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC), told reporters in eastern Burma when asked about the U.S. decision to ban new American investment in Burma.
Khin Nyunt, who is also the powerful military intelligence chief, also denied Western allegations of human rights abuses.
But exiled dissidents in Thailand applauded the U.S. move.

"This means the U.S. supports our struggle for democracy and they care about the suffering of the Burmese people," said Aung Myo Myo, of the National Coalition Government of the Union of Burma (NCGUB) - a self-described Burmese government in exile.
The NCGUB and other exile groups in Thailand and elsewhere have urged the United States and other governments to stop investing in Burma because of human rights abuses there.

Roger Beach, chairman of oil and gas company Unocal Corp -- the largest American investor in Burma -- said on Tuesday the sanctions were counterproductive but said it would not impact Unocal's investment in the region.

"If it's true, we are terribly disappointed because we feel that engaging in other infrastructure projects for Myanmar (Burma) at this time would be very beneficial to the development of the economy of Myanmar," Beach said during a visit to Bangkok. He was waiting for further details on the sanctions.
The SLORC has been accused by human right groups and Western governments of abuses like summary executions, using forced labour and employing repressive tactics against the opposition.

The State Department will officially announce the sanctions banning new U.S. investment in Burma later on Tuesday, officials in Washington said. The United States is the fourth largest investor in Burma in terms of approved investment.

But some diplomats questioned if the sanctions would help the situation in the impoverished Southeast Asian nation. They said retaliatory measures imposed by the SLORC may actually worsen the lives of opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi and members of her National League for Democracy (NLD) party.
"The question we have to ask now is how will they retaliate," said a Rangoon-based diplomat.
"What will the SLORC do? Will they direct their retaliation against the U.S. or will they move against Aung San Suu Kyi and the opposition?" the diplomat asked.

The U.S. sanctions were approved by the Senate late last year following a series of crackdowns on Suu Kyi and the NLD. The SLORC has also been condemned for failing to recognise the landslide 1990 electoral victory of the NLD which was co-founded and now led by Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi.
Thousands of NLD supporters were detained last year, and Suu Kyi was put under virtual house arrest in December following rare student demonstrations in Rangoon.
Suu Kyi, who was under official house arrest for six years until 1995 for her outspoken attacks on the government, has publicly supported sanctions and urged foreigners not to invest in Burma.
Some diplomats said the SLORC was likely to retaliate soon.
"It depends on how much this has taken them by surprise, since sanctions have been on the cards for some time," one said.
Other diplomats said the SLORC might be wary of making any major moves while Burma awaits full membership in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Burma, Cambodia and Laos are expected to be admitted to the seven-nation group this year, possibly in July.
International pressure has mounted on ASEAN not to admit Burma but the group follows a "constructive engagement" policy and has said it will not interfere in politics of another nation.
"But this could put pressure on ASEAN to really decide which way they want to go," one diplomat said.
Beach of Unocal told a business luncheon on Tuesday that sanctions were ineffective and hurt people, not regimes.

"In numerous countries, sanctions have had the effect of hurting the poor the most," he told the American Chamber of Commerce. "Sanctions...hurt people. And they cut off American companies from places in the world where we should be involved."
